html:
Kanem-Bornu was an empire around Lake Chad in central Africa that lasted, under one royal line or another, from about 700 to 1893. It was one of the longest-lived states anywhere in the world. It was centred first on Kanem, east of the lake, and from the late 14th century on Bornu, to the west.

The first rulers, the Duguwa, ruled from Njimi in Kanem with the title mai. The state lived from the trans-Saharan trade, controlling the route north across the desert to the Fezzan and Libya. It sent out salt, ivory and enslaved people captured in raids to the south.

Its history in phases:

  • Islam. In the 11th century the court became Muslim and a new dynasty, the Sayfawa, took over. It ruled for some eight hundred years.
  • Kanem's height. Under Mai Dunama Dibalemi in the 13th century its power reached far into the Sahara.
  • The move to Bornu. In the 14th century wars with the Bilala people drove the court out of Kanem. Mai Umar re-founded it in Bornu, and after a century of turmoil Ali Gaji built a new capital, Ngazargamu, in the late 15th century.
  • Bornu's height. Idris Alooma, in the late 16th century, retook Kanem and bought firearms and Turkish musketeers through contacts with the Ottoman Empire.

In the early 19th century the jihad that created the Sokoto Caliphate sacked Ngazargamu. A scholar, Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi, led the defence and his family took real power, ending the Sayfawa line in 1846. In 1893 the warlord Rabih az-Zubayr conquered Bornu, and soon after Britain, France and Germany divided its lands between Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon. Al-Kanemi's descendant, the Shehu of Borno, still holds a traditional title in Nigeria.
